title: Name it first
hook: the Buddha names suffering first, the way a doctor names an illness (Samyutta Nikaya 56.11)
carry: stand next to it and look

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was sabr, patience that holds under trial, one of four answers to why we suffer. Your line was each answers differently. Today, inside the Buddha's answer.

"It's making a noise." "What kind of noise?" "A bad one." "When does it happen?" "I don't know, sometimes." A mechanic can't do a thing with that. A grinding when you brake, a click when you turn left: once the noise has a plain name, the work can start. It's easy to treat our own troubles the other way round. We fix, we distract, we explain, and we never quite say what the noise is. The Buddha's first teaching starts somewhere else. It starts by naming.
screen: `WHAT KIND OF NOISE?` → `NAMED PLAINLY, THEN FIXED.` → `THE BUDDHA STARTS BY NAMING.`

segments.voice: First, a plain list. In the Samyutta Nikaya, the Buddha's first teaching lays out four noble truths, and the first is suffering, dukkha. He doesn't describe it with drama. He lists it: birth is suffering, aging is suffering, illness is suffering, death is suffering. So are being joined with what you dislike, being parted from what you love, and not getting what you want. Second, look at that last one. Not getting what you want sits on the same list as death, without ranking. A canceled plan and a funeral can both find a place there. Third, the first task is to understand it. In the same teaching, each truth comes with its own job. Suffering is to be fully understood. Its origin is to be let go. Its ending is to be realized. The path is to be developed. So the first job the Buddha gives suffering isn't fix it, escape it or explain it away. It's understand it, all the way through. Teachers sometimes use a picture for this: a good doctor names the illness before writing the prescription. Fourth, named before it's fixed. A name is a small thing, but it changes where you stand. When the trouble is a fog, you're inside it. When it has a plain name, aging, illness, being parted from someone, not getting what I wanted, you can stand next to it and look. The cause, the ending and the path all come later. In the Buddha's order, naming comes first.
screen: `A PLAIN LIST, NO DRAMA.` · `EVEN NOT GETTING WHAT YOU WANT.` · `THE FIRST TASK: UNDERSTAND IT.` · `NAMED BEFORE IT'S FIXED.` · then, large: `NAME IT FIRST.`

segments.voice: Find one pain you're carrying right now, in the body, in a relationship, or a small frustration from this morning, and name it plainly, the way the old list does: this is worry about money; this is missing my brother; this is a sore back. No because, no should, no story; if the story starts, come back to the plain name. Then sit beside it the way you'd sit beside a friend on a bench, close but not inside their trouble.
Dukkha, the Buddha's word for suffering, from birth and aging to not getting what you want, named plainly so it can be understood. Today's word.
Your line: stand next to it and look. A plain name comes before any fix. Day seven hundred, done.

howItsDone: Buddhists learn the four noble truths as the heart of the Buddha's first teaching, and some meditation teachers begin by asking students to notice and name their experience plainly before trying to change it.

chat.says: Why would the Buddha start with suffering? Isn't that kind of gloomy?
options: He names it plainly first, because its first task is to be understood.
He starts there because suffering must be fixed fast, before anything else.
He starts there because only big griefs count; small upsets don't belong.
chat.meaning: In his first teaching each truth has a task, and suffering's is to be fully understood. Naming it plainly comes before any fix.

SN 56.11 paraphrased: the first truth's list (birth, aging, illness, death; union with the displeasing, separation from the pleasing, not getting what one wants) and its summary in the five aggregates of clinging, which is left out for length. Confirm the list.
The four tasks (dukkha pariññeyya, samudaya pahātabba, nirodha sacchikātabba, magga bhāvetabba) are from the same sutta; confirm the English glosses.
The doctor comparison is offered as 'a picture teachers sometimes use', not as the sutta's own image; confirm that framing. Day 240 used the same picture, so it is kept to one line here.
